analysis.one_liner: Bans junk food from school vending machines and snack lines by updating outdated federal nutrition standards.
analysis.headline: With 157 cosponsors including 7 Republicans, the bill never advanced past a House subcommittee referral and died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal rules already require school lunches and breakfasts to meet nutrition standards, and since 1979 the government has banned the sale of foods with almost no nutritional value where school meals are served. But those rules did not cover food sold elsewhere on campus — vending machines, snack bars, school stores, and a la carte lines — and the definition of 'junk food' had not been updated since 1979. This bill would have directed the Department of Agriculture to rewrite that definition using current nutrition science and apply it to all food sold on school grounds during the school day, with a possible exemption for occasional school fundraisers.
analysis.who_benefits: Schoolchildren, who would no longer be surrounded by candy, soda, and snack food for sale all day at school; parents trying to keep their kids on a healthy diet; and the federal school meal programs, whose investment in balanced meals would no longer be undercut by junk food sold a few feet away. The bill's own findings note that childhood obesity has quadrupled among ages 6 to 11 since 1963, only 2 percent of children eat a diet consistent with federal recommendations, and obesity costs the country an estimated $117 billion a year [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Agriculture to revise the definition of 'food of minimal nutritional value' within 180 days, using current science on calories, saturated fat, trans fat, sodium, added sugars, and the links between diet and obesity and chronic disease [S2][S3].

Extends the revised ban to all food sold outside the school meal programs, anywhere on the school campus, at any time during the school day — closing the loophole that let vending machines, school stores, snack bars, and a la carte lines sell foods that would be banned in the lunchroom [S2][S3].

Allows only a narrow, at-the-Agriculture-Department's-discretion exemption for infrequent school-sponsored fundraisers, and explicitly excludes vending machines, school stores, snack bars, and a la carte sales from any such exemption [S3].
If the Department fails to issue final rules within a year, the proposed rules automatically become final, preventing the update from stalling in the bureaucracy [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Snack food and beverage companies, which would lose a captive school-day market in vending machines, stores, and snack bars. School districts and parent groups would also lose some revenue from on-campus snack and a la carte sales that helps fund activities, though the bill allows limited exemptions for infrequent, school-approved fundraisers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Snack and beverage companies; school fundraisers

drawbacks.text: Schools and parent-teacher groups raise real money from snack sales, vending commissions, and a la carte lines; a campus-wide ban would cut into that revenue, which is why the bill lets the Department grant exemptions for infrequent school-approved fundraisers but only outside vending machines, stores, and snack bars [S3].

Enforcement ties the ban to federal school meal funding, meaning a school out of compliance could put its federal lunch and breakfast reimbursements at risk, and schools would bear the administrative burden of applying one nutrition standard to every food sale on campus [S2][S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that banning foods at school does not by itself change what children eat at home or elsewhere, so the health benefits depend on how strict the Department's new definition turns out to be [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong and the costs are modest and partly addressed in the bill itself: the fundraiser exemption preserves some school revenue, and the burden falls mainly on companies selling low-nutrition food to a captive audience of children. The main design risk is that the outcome would depend entirely on how strictly the Department of Agriculture wrote the new definition, and tying enforcement to federal meal funding could pressure cash-strapped schools.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, then passed to a subcommittee two months later, and nothing further ever happened before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lynn Woolsey (D-CA) introduced the bill on March 6, 2007, joined by Rep. Christopher Shays (R-CT), and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1][S3][S5].

On June 27, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Healthy Families and Communities; the record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 110th Congress [S5].
The bill drew 157 cosponsors — 150 Democrats and 7 Republicans — support substantial enough that it could plausibly have passed if it had ever reached the floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Snack food and beverage companies kept their school vending and snack-line sales, and nothing changed for children's nutrition: the 1979 definition remained in force.

for.name: Rep. Lynn Woolsey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 157 cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Joined Woolsey in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee leadership
against.role: Committee chaired by Rep. George Miller (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it was passed to the Subcommittee on Healthy Families and Communities and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Snack food and vending industry
against.role: Companies selling soda, candy, and snacks through school vending machines, stores, and snack bars
against.what_they_did: The industry publicly opposed extending nutrition standards to all competitive foods sold on school campuses during this period.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic (150 of 157 cosponsors) but included 7 Republicans, and the bill itself was co-introduced by a Democrat and a Republican.

industries.note: These companies sell candy, soda, and chips to children through school vending machines, stores, snack bars, and a la carte lines. The bill would have barred foods of minimal nutritional value from all of those outlets during the school day, eliminating a captive daily market.

industries.industry: School fundraising and a la carte food operations
industries.note: Schools and parent groups rely on snack and vending revenue for activities and supplies. The bill allowed the Department to exempt infrequent, school-approved fundraisers but excluded vending machines, school stores, and snack bars from that exemption, so most routine snack revenue would still be lost.
